title: Feeding a sourdough starter, daily rhythm
subtitle: How to maintain an active starter at room temperature
excerpt: A sourdough starter kept at room temperature needs feeding once a day to stay healthy. Discard half, add fresh flour and water, and the culture resets its cycle. The daily rhythm keeps the yeast strong and the acid levels balanced.
sourceNotes: Feeding ratios and timing based on standard room-temperature maintenance schedules used in home sourdough baking. The 1:1:1 (starter:flour:water) ratio is a widely taught starting point.

glossaryTerms.definition: The portion of starter removed before each feeding. Discarding prevents the culture from becoming too acidic and the jar from overflowing. Discard can be used in crackers, pancakes, or flatbreads.
The proportion of fresh flour and water added relative to the remaining starter. A 1:1:1 ratio means equal weights of starter, flour, and water.

Add 50 g strong white flour and 50 g water at room temperature (about 21°C). Stir well until no dry flour remains.
Mark the jar with a rubber band or elastic at the current level. Replace the lid loosely. Leave at room temperature.

A healthy starter rises to roughly double its fed volume within 4 to 8 hours at 21°C, then falls back. The peak is the best time to bake. If you feed in the morning, the starter is usually ready to use by mid-afternoon. If you miss a day, the starter does not die, it becomes more acidic. Feed it twice in one day to bring it back to strength.

In a warm kitchen (above 24°C), the starter may need feeding twice a day. A cold kitchen (below 18°C) slows the cycle; feeding every 36 hours may suffice. When you bake less often, move the starter to the fridge and feed weekly instead.
Discard straight from the jar works in any quick bread where you would otherwise add plain flour: pancakes, crumpets, flatbreads, crackers. It adds a mild tang without needing to be active.
